A negative claim about the source, but one the full source text bears out: the review nowhere ranks George and Walter above the other shows, and distributes its strongest enthusiasm elsewhere — 'I love it' (Rothschild upstairs), 'It's brilliantly gloopy, messy, cartoonish, chaotic and satirical' (Fitzpatrick), 'they're amazing images' (Hasegawa) — while the Ingleby show is merely 'good, too'. The absence of the ranking is verifiable in the evidence supplied.
The article stating its own reason for pairing two cases. Causal form is not itself evidence of anything; the causation is about the article's method, not about the world.

Source: 'often with her young son'. The article preserves the 'often' qualifier.

Verbatim: 'to tell them clearly'.

A framing device introducing the article's reading of the review's recurring vocabulary. The recurrence itself is grounded (see P57-P61); naming it 'the festival's characteristic verb' is the article's own move.

A frequency claim about the source, and the source bears it out repeatedly: 'undiscovered archives', 'you'll have uncovered so many hidden stories', 'was only discovered after her death', 'Another largely undiscovered artist', 'this previously undiscovered marginalised artist', 'loads of hidden stories and undiscovered narratives'.

The source does invoke this figure: 'You've just got to follow your nose and hope you sniff out something you like.' The presence of the word 'visitor' in the proposition decides nothing; the predicate is what the review invokes, and it is licensed.

Licensed twice over: the quoted scolding, '"You've never heard of this previously undiscovered marginalised artist? You bastard!"', and 'it's all a bit worthy and lecture-y, like you're getting told off in every gallery you enter'.

An evaluation of the role a word plays in the source, resting on the recurrence established at P57-P61. It attributes no specific statement, ranking or omission to the review beyond what the text shows, so it adds no new factual state about the source.
A reading of what the word tracks, built from the review's account of wandering the festival. No fact asserted.

All three venues are named in the source as festival venues one enters: 'her show at City Art Gallery', 'The group show at Ingleby Gallery', 'at Custom Lane'. The concrete details are licensed; the walking-in is the source's own generic frame.

The extraction returned no anchor, but the source supplies one for this specific predicate: 'You can't walk into a gallery without learning about some subcultural genius or longlost creative you've never heard of.' Prior ignorance of the artist licenses that the images could not be anticipated. Unlike P19, nothing is asserted about what the visitor brought.
The article's analysis of where the review locates discovery. Reasoning about the material; no new factual state.
Continues the same reading, drawing on the source's second-person present-tense framing of the visit. No fact added.

The anchor is the review's second-person prescription, 'You've just got to follow your nose', not a first-person statement of route. But the review is a first-person account ('I love it', 'I'd be lying', 'we can all go home happy. I did.') that moves show to show without a system, having said no system is available. Reading the prescription as describing the reviewer's own route is a reading of grounded material; it introduces no name, date, place or event the source lacks.

Rests on 'EAF is too big and complex, with too many moving parts and collaborations and clashing ideas to really make sense' and the source's own description of a 'city-wide art festival'. Transposing scale from festival to city is the article's reading, not a new fact.
Connective instruction to the reader. Asserts nothing.
Verbatim: 'she never showed her work publicly in her lifetime'.
Source: 'was only discovered after her death in 2013'. 'Found after 2013' asserts no more than the anchor.
Source: 'who died having never shown any of the thousands of paintings and drawings he amassed over his lifetime'. The source itself uses 'any', so the unqualified form is licensed here.

The review says 'MOST of the Japanese illustrator's work, you guessed it, stayed unpublished and unseen in his lifetime.' The proposition attributes to the review an unqualified claim about his work with the quantifier dropped. The anchor supports a strictly weaker statement than the one attributed, so the attribution misstates the source.

Same defect as a claim about the world: the source licenses only that MOST of Hasegawa's work stayed unpublished and unseen. Asserting it of his work without qualification is a factual state the evidence does not license, and it is stated as settled.

A reading of how the source deploys the word, and the deployments are on the page: 'you'll have uncovered so many hidden stories', 'you've never heard of', 'this previously undiscovered marginalised artist' — all addressed to the person arriving. The article characterises grounded usage rather than adding a new fact about the review.
Continues the semantic reading of the word. No factual state asserted.

The extraction returned no anchor, but the source licenses this state directly: 'some subcultural genius or longlost creative you've never heard of', reinforced by 'undiscovered archives' and 'previously undiscovered'. Prior non-knowledge of the work is exactly what the source asserts of the visitor.

A negative claim, but about what a word can carry, and the source's own usages bear it out: every instance of the discovery family marks a coming-to-light ('only discovered after her death', 'largely undiscovered artist'), while the years of non-showing are named separately and in plain terms ('never showed her work publicly in her lifetime'). This is the article reasoning about grounded vocabulary, not attributing an unevidenced statement or omission to the review.
An observation drawn from the two date ranges the source supplies (1957-2013, 1926-2009). Article-level reasoning about grounded facts.

Combines two grounded facts — 'she never showed her work publicly in her lifetime' and Walter 'died having never shown any of the thousands of paintings and drawings he amassed over his lifetime' — with the supplied lifespans. The synthesis is the article's; no new name, date or number is introduced.
